title: How to Become a More Approachable Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece takes issue with the conventional account of approachability as warmth and an open door, and relocates it in something counterintuitive: restraint about answering. It offers a formula, Q + A x X = < Q, glossed as questions followed by answers in repetition producing fewer questions over time, and concedes this is hard for capable leaders to accept, since a good answer feels like the obviously correct response to a question. The mechanism it describes is that fluent answers leave team members feeling instructed rather than engaged, and that the pattern quietly trains people out of raising things at all. Underneath sits a claim about why people ask in the first place, that colleagues only occasionally want an answer and more often want perspective, insight and a chance to offer their own reading. The behavioural prescription is to meet a question by exploring it, clarifying, probing and elucidating, rather than closing it. The closing formulation, that when others feel they can engage they approach, makes engagement the cause and approachability the effect.
points: The argument inverts the usual advice: approachability is produced less by warmth and open doors than by a leader's willingness to withhold the answer they already have.
The formula Q + A x X = < Q names a specific decay mechanism, that repeated quick answering measurably reduces the number of questions a leader subsequently receives.
The diagnosis of why this happens is that capable answers leave people feeling instructed rather than engaged, so the cost of being helpful is paid in future information flow.
The underlying claim about motive is the load-bearing one: colleagues usually ask to gain perspective and offer their own spin, not to obtain a correct answer.
The practical substitute is named as a set of moves rather than a disposition, clarifying, probing, questioning and elucidating whatever is brought to you.
quotes: Becoming a more approachable leader is about more than listening to others and maintaining an open door. It is most about refraining from giving answers and advice too quickly.
Translated, this means questions followed by answers in repetition results in fewer questions.
When facile leaders are quick with smart answers, team members feel instructed but not engaged.
Unbeknownst to many leaders, colleagues only occasionally ask questions to receive an answer.
Instead, they ask questions to gain perspective and insight, while also offering their own spin.
Clarifying, probing, questioning, and elucidating on any topic brought to them is how the best leaders make themselves more approachable.
